title: test-0011-SCI-BIO-LIVING
passage: In the vast Thar Desert, a camel survives extreme heat by storing fat in its hump, not liquid water, which provides energy for long journeys. Nearby, a cactus plant stands still, yet it is very much alive. Unlike a dry seed that remains dormant, the cactus is actively respiring, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide both day and night, even while it photosynthesizes. The spines on a cactus are actually modified leaves that reduce water loss through transpiration, while also serving as a defense against hungry herbivores. In the same ecosystem, a desert fish survives in small pools by using its gills to extract dissolved oxygen from the water, rather than swallowing it to create air. The habitat of these organisms is not just the living creatures, but also the sandy soil, the intense sunlight, and the dry air that surround them. These abiotic factors are essential components of the environment. Even though the cactus does not walk or run, it responds to the sun by orienting its growth, proving that movement from place to place is not the only sign of life. Every organism here, from the smallest seed to the largest camel, is part of a complex, living system that interacts constantly with its non-living surroundings to maintain its existence.
